tasks.plan:
## Overview

Generate contract registry markdown from the compiled Zod contract modules so schema docs can be refreshed deterministically instead of being hand-maintained. The generator uses `compiled/contracts/` as the build output path because `tsconfig.contracts.json` currently emits there, despite the older backlog wording mentioning `dist/contracts/`.

## Phases

1. Add `scripts/generate-registries.js` to introspect the compiled contract modules.
2. Add `npm run generate:registries` and a `--check` drift mode.
3. Regenerate/merge the WebSocket and backlog registry sections while preserving manual gap and audit notes.
4. Generate new `tool-schemas.md` and `mcp-envelopes.md` registries and list them in the registry README.
5. Verify contract compilation, generated output stability, and policy tests.

tasks.title: Memory importance scoring at write time
tasks.description: Initial strength should reflect memory importance rather than always defaulting to 1.0. The Codex extraction prompt should score each memory 1-5 by type (decision=5, preference=4, feedback=4, pattern=3, fact=2 as defaults). Map score to initial strength in the 0.6-1.0 range so high-signal memories decay slower from birth. Patch addMemory() and addMemories() in lib/memory.js to accept an importance field and set initial strength accordingly. Update the Codex extraction prompt in extractSessionToKnowledge() to request and return importance scores alongside each memory.
tasks.plan: Add importance-aware memory writes without changing retrieval or decay behavior. The memory module normalizes explicit importance scores to 1-5, defaults by type when absent, stores the importance value, and maps it to initial strength in the 0.6-1.0 range. The session extractor prompt now asks for an importance score alongside each memory and passes it through to Firestore writes. Focused tests cover default scoring, clamping, and strength mapping.

proofUnits.expectedPassingEvidence: Vitest passes memory importance scoring tests in test/memory/memory.test.js.

proofUnits.expectedPassingEvidence: Tests prove importance 1-5 maps to 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, and 1.0 respectively, and code inspection shows both write paths call initialStrengthForMemory().

tasks.title: Memory consolidation synthesis — deduplication on write
tasks.description: Before writing new memories from Codex extraction, compare each candidate against existing project memories using Jaccard similarity on tags plus substring overlap on content. Merge near-duplicates (similarity above 0.7) by reinforcing the existing memory rather than creating a new document. Prevents the collection from filling with restatements of the same facts across sessions. Fetch existing memories once per extraction batch, score all candidates against them, and split candidates into new writes vs reinforcements before committing.
tasks.plan: Add write-time memory deduplication to the batch memory write path. New pure helpers compute tag Jaccard similarity, normalized substring overlap, combined memory similarity, duplicate selection, and a consolidation plan that splits candidates into writes versus reinforcements. addMemories() now fetches active existing memories once per project in the batch, reinforces near-duplicates above the 0.7 threshold, writes only new memories, and suppresses repeated candidates inside the same extraction batch.

proofUnits.expectedInitialFailure: Before this change, memory.js had no similarity helpers or duplicate detection functions.
proofUnits.expectedPassingEvidence: Vitest passes tests for jaccardSimilarity(), substringOverlap(), memorySimilarity(), and findDuplicateMemory().

proofUnits.title: Batch consolidation splits writes from reinforcements

proofUnits.expectedPassingEvidence: Tests prove planMemoryConsolidation() returns one reinforcement and one write for mixed batches.

proofUnits.expectedPassingEvidence: Tests prove repeated candidates produce one write and one reinforcement plan item.

tasks.title: Memory editing and correction UI
tasks.description: Provide a path for Scott to flag, edit, or manually archive a specific memory. Codex misextractions currently persist until natural decay (weeks). A Polaris panel listing memories by project with inline edit and archive controls closes the human feedback loop on extraction quality. The panel should show content, type, tags, strength, accessCount, and age. Editing a memory resets its strength to the importance-based initial value; archiving sets _archived: true immediately.
tasks.plan: Add a human correction loop for Firestore memories inside the existing Memory panel. The memory module now exposes list, edit, and archive helpers; server WebSocket handlers list active project/global memories and protect edit/archive writes with the UI token; the Memory panel lets Scott select a project, include global memories, edit content/type/tags/importance inline, and archive bad memories immediately. Editing resets strength using the importance-based initial strength calculation so corrected memories re-enter retrieval with the right durability.

tasks.title: Bi-temporal audit log schema for security tooling (design constraint)
tasks.description: Forward reference and design constraint for future Polaris security tools. Any security audit log system built on top of the memory/knowledge infrastructure must use bi-temporal structure: valid_time (when the fact was true in the real world) and transaction_time (when Polaris recorded it). This enables forensic past-state reconstruction: given an arbitrary past moment T, reconstruct exactly what the system knew and what was true, independently. Critical for answering Were we secure at T vs Did we think we were secure at T -- a meaningful distinction for CMMC, HIPAA, and SOC2 compliance. Compound condition detection: graph traversal over bi-temporal edges can find attack windows where multiple conditions overlapped (e.g. suspended account + live access edge = breach window during interval [T1, T2]). Schema sketch: { entityId, attribute, value, validFrom, validTo, txFrom, txTo }. Do not build this as a flat log -- the temporal indexing is load-bearing.

tasks.title: Isolate backlog writes from the shared primary repo (concurrency hazard)
tasks.description: Multiple parallel sessions edit docs/backlog.json in the shared primary repo (C:\Users\scott\Code\Polaris) on main at the same time. During task #51 planning, an uncommitted backlog edit was swept into another session's commit (ccf9278) and the working tree briefly showed tasks from 3+ sessions at once (in-flight #56/#59). Fix: backlog reads/writes performed by skills (plan-task, start-build, finish-build, status transitions) should operate in an isolated worktree pinned to a freshly-fetched origin/main, mutate atomically, and push HEAD:main with rebase-on-reject — never edit the shared primary working tree directly. Prevents lost/misattributed backlog changes and task-number collisions.
plan: Harden every backlog-writing command around a disposable worktree created from freshly fetched origin/main instead of the shared primary working tree.
Require Node fs utf8 JSON writes, exact task-number mutation reapplication after rebase conflicts, push HEAD:main without force, and cleanup of the disposable worktree.
Sync the command source files from ~/.claude/commands into docs/skills so Polaris documentation mirrors the executable skill instructions.
Keep read-only build/review skills from checking out main just to inspect backlog state by using git show origin/main:docs/backlog.json or the same disposable worktree pattern.

tasks.title: Orchestrator skill: multi-session conflict detection
tasks.description: Build /orchestrate — a universal Claude Code skill that monitors open PRs across all active sessions for a project, detects file-set intersections, classifies conflict types (additive / same-line / correctness divergence), and writes merger guides to Obsidian. Invoked automatically when a second session opens on the same project. General-first with per-project config block.

objective.statement: Provide Scott with automatic cross-session visibility into file-set conflicts between parallel build sessions, so conflicts are detected before PR review rather than at merge time.
successCriteria: Orchestrator session auto-spawns with title "Project Orchestrator" when a project reaches 2 active sessions
Orchestrator session auto-closes when the last session on a project closes
Init builds file-set watch list for all active branches, including branches with no open PR
Monitor loop refreshes watch list on new commits before running intersection check
Burst GIT:COMMITS events within one tick window are debounced to a single analysis run
File-set intersection triggers conflict classification and merger guide written to Obsidian
Dependency-violation alert fires when a task starts before its blocking PR is merged
Orchestrator card displays amber-gold pulsing glow, absent on all other session cards
nonGoals: Full orchestrator status panel in UI

tasks.plan:
## Overview

Build /orchestrate: a universal Claude Code skill that monitors all active session branches for a
project, detects file-set intersections between branches, classifies conflict types (additive /
same-line / correctness-divergence), and writes merger guides to Obsidian. Auto-spawned by server.js
as a dedicated chat session when a project reaches 2 active sessions; torn down when the last session closes.

## Phases

Phase 0: Spike -- validate spawnMaxChat auto-invocation mechanism
Phase 1: server.js orchestrator lifecycle (per-project session-count map, spawn at 2, teardown at 0,
         dedup guard, title "Project Orchestrator")
Phase 2: orchestrate.md scaffold + init (CLAUDE.md startup, gh pr list, git diff watch list, gh failure handling)
Phase 3: Monitor loop (health monitor pattern, 30s default, collect-and-flush debounce,
         GIT:COMMITS refresh, BACKLOG:CHANGED dep check, REGISTRY:CHANGED note)
Phase 4: Conflict classification engine (additive / same-line / correctness-divergence via git diff deep read)
Phase 5: Output artifacts + UI (status table, merger guide to Obsidian, dep-violation alert,
         mockup.html amber-gold pulsing glow CSS 2.5s)
Phase 6: Fixture branches + end-to-end proof run

## First Proof Unit

Open a second session on any project; "Project Orchestrator" session card with pulsing amber-gold
glow appears within 2s. Verified via manual observation in Polaris UI.
